utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, could you call the case, please, Madam?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, gentlemen. Yes, I can follow the proceedings in my mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and also good morning to my learned friends of the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I'm here together with co-counsel, Mrs. Patricia Sellers, and our case manager, Mrs. Donnica Henry-Frijlink, and later on,, with apologies, also counsel Gramsci di Fazio will join the team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good morning to you and your team. Present and future. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Vasvija Vidovic. Good morning to my friends from the Prosecution. Together with Mr. John Jones I'm representing Mr. Naser Oric, and together we have our legal assistant, Ms. Adisa Mehic and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Madam, and good morning to you and your team. While we are at preliminaries, let us go for a little while in private session because I need to give some information, confidential information, to the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. On Friday, as you know, Defence filed an urgent request for certification of the Trial Chamber's confidential decision on second Defence motion for protective measures for Witness D002. When are we hopefully expecting the response? I think I left a message that this is urgent, not just from the motion itself but also because the witness is amongst those which is listed to be coming over shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we intend to file our response by tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. If you could file it by this evening, it will be better.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: We do our best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because we will be having meetings on several issues, the three judges, tomorrow and if it's on our table by the end of the day then we can deal with it first thing tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we do our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then later on, this week, we hope to be able to give you our decision on whether the late disclosure of C4 and C6 was in violation of -- by the Prosecution was in violation of Rule 68. The -- is there a problem? No problem? All right. I'm still waiting for a document from the Registrar's office detailing the procedure or the protocol they would expect, which will not be binding on us, but I mean, it's for our information and more or less for information purposes and then we decide, what the procedure for allowing exhibits to be examined by forensic teams outside of the Netherlands. I don't know if it has been done before here but if it has been done, I will get details of the procedure and of course then I will let you both parties but particularly Madam Vidovic and Mr. Jones. We are still waiting, unless it has been filed in these last couple of days, your reply to the Prosecution's response on the Rule 70 matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, we have filed a reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When did you file it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I believe Friday. It may only actually be going through the system today but we filed on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't seen it anyway and I haven't been informed of it in any case. Then I think, having handed down our decision on Avdo Huseinovic, you need to decide whether to bring him over or not. That's up to you. We're not going to involve ourselves in that. But -- we are awaiting your motion regarding the two witnesses Hans Vlens and Rene Caravielhe.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, and that raises issues related to what we discussed earlier. It's one of the reasons for the delay. But it will be, I imagine, within certainly a fortnight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I think that covers the preliminaries that we needed to raise. Any preliminaries on your part?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's about a year ago that the issues has been discussed about an interview by Murat Efendic of alleged to be Naser Oric and that was a year ago. We were able to provide the Trial Chamber, as you might recall, a transcript but there was no video of it and so we did do some actions in that respect and we can now confirm that we could track the video and we will disclose it as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben. Madam Vidovic, any preliminaries on your part?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just in regard with Mr. Murat Efendic, we know that there was a video of his interview but that's not what it's about. We are expecting the audio material of the transcript that we received. So we are not talking about audio -- video material but audiotapes. We know about the existence of the video material but that has nothing to do with the transcript in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, to inform the parties, the video of course include images, footage and audio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's happening to -- okay. All right. It's leveled down because I was hearing -- all right. But, Ms. Vidovic, when we get this video we will see what the position is. I mean -- of course if you have issues to raise arising out of the filing of the video or the availability of that video, we'll deal with it at that time. Can we bring in the witness? Yes. Registrar, 28th, we are still sitting in the afternoon, make again another effort to see if we could sit in the morning because we will have to rise early on the 28th if we sit in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then I explain -- I will explain to the parties why the three of us have to rise early, stop early, the sitting on the 28th, if we sit in the afternoon. So good morning to you, Mr. Malagic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You should be, and I take it that you are, receiving interpretation of what I'm saying in English in your own language, which enables you to follow the proceedings. If at any time there is something wrong with the reception of interpretation, either you're not receiving it or it's too loud or you can't hear it, or too low, please draw our attention straight away so that we'll rectify the problem. You are about to start giving evidence in this case against Naser Oric. You are a Defence witness. And our rules require that before you start giving evidence, you enter a -- you make a solemn declaration equivalent to an oath in several domestic jurisdictions, consisting in a commitment on your part to speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth throughout the entire testimony. The text of the solemn declaration is going to be handed to you now. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us that you will be testifying the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Malagic. Please do take a seat, make yourself comfortable. Have you ever given testimony before in your life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll explain to you a little bit briefly the whole procedure. Usher, please make sure that it is not in the way of Madam Vidovic. As I said, you are a Defence witness and very soon you will start answering the questions that will be put to you, first by Madam Vidovic, who is lead counsel for Naser Oric, and then by Ms. Sellers, who is co-counsel in the Prosecution team. Let me introduce myself. I am the presiding Judge in this trial. My name is Carmel Agius and I come from Malta. To my right I have Judge Hans Henrik Brydensholt from the Kingdom of Denmark. To my left I have Judge Professor Albin Eser from Republic of Germany. Together we are presiding over this trial. We are the three of us professional judges. You are expected to be here for two or three days. There is a chance of staying here even longer if instead of answering the questions that are put to you, you try to give more information than is required from you. Whether you will go back home in time as expected pretty much depends on you. I can assure you that the lawyers will do their best to be very concise and very precise in the questions and the information that they need from you but it is the tendency of many witnesses to volunteer more information than what is being asked from them. We don't want more information. So please, my advice to you and my recommendation to you is that in the course of the questioning, both from Madam Vidovic and from Ms. Sellers, you answer the question, the whole question and nothing but the question. Did I make myself clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The last thing, I know that Madam Vidovic would have explained this to you but I'm explaining it also is that both you and Madam Vidovic speak the same language, and if you don't allow a small pause, small interval of time, both of you, between questions and answer, you will create a lot of problems to our interpreters, who have already got a very difficult job in interpreting into Serbo-Croat, into English and into French while the words are being spoken, and if you rush and jump to put questions or answer questions without allowing this short interval of time, we won't have all the transcript that we require. There will be problems. So between Madam Vidovic's questions and your answer, please allow a short interval of time so that the interpreters in the meantime would have translated the words into English and into French. Okay. Mr. Malagic, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Malagic.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to respond to my questions as briefly as possible, as was explained to you by Your Honour. Mr. Malagic, could you please state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: My full name is Azir Malagic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were born on the 1st of July of 1967 in Voljavica, municipality of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your father's name is Enes, your mother's is Saliha and her maiden name was Salihovic?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your sister's name is Revda, and you have three brothers, Senad, Reuf, and Hajrudin?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You completed your primary education in Voljavica and then in Bratunac in 1982; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You completed your secondary education in 1986 in Ljubovija and there was an agricultural school?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, it might be easier for you if you moved your chair closer to the microphones. Thank you. You served your military term in Kraljevo in Serbia from 1986 to 1987?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In 1999, you started studying at the school of political science in Sarajevo and you haven't completed your degree yet?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were employed in 1991 in Bratunac and you worked there for only six months in Oka enterprise?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You spent the war in the area of Srebrenica and Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When Srebrenica fell, your father went missing, together with around 20 members of your extended family?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After the war, you became a professional soldier with the army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You underwent military training under the auspices of the government of the United States?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You are now employed with the military school in Tuzla as sergeant first class, and you teach the recruits who have come to serve their military term and you cover the subject of artillery?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to put a map before the witness. We will use this map throughout the testimony. It is a map of the Srebrenica area.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please mark some of the villages on the map that I will ask you to point to us? Could the witness please use our pen? Witness, I believe the map is in front of you. Please mark Srebrenica for the Trial Chamber. Then Likari. Then your own village of Voljavica.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please mark for the Chamber the village of Zaluzje next. Then Prisoj, Biljaca, Lasovac, Poloznik, Pirici, a bit further there is Dimnici. Could you please mark that? Predola. Petinici. Lokva. And Potocari. Please explain to the Trial Chamber what was the ethnic makeup of these villages prior to the war.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. These villages were exclusively inhabited by the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please point out to the villages of Pobrdje now, Rakovac, Bjelovac, Sikiric, Sase, Gradina, Kostanovice, Neskovici, and Zalazje. Could you please tell us the ethnic makeup of those villages prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: The villages of Pobrdje, Bjelovac, Sikiric, Sase and Gradina, the population there was mixed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And Kostanovice, Neskovici and Zaluzje?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Kostanovice, Neskovici and Zaluzje, those villages were exclusively populated by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your native Voljavica, prior to the war, was that exclusively a Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, only Muslims lived in Voljavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we please assign an exhibit number to this map as a Defence Exhibit? And I would kindly ask the witness to keep the map because we will be referring to it throughout the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, Madam Vidovic. This will be D7 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D757, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you initial this map in one of its corners? You can initial or sign.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: [Witness complies].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If it's easier, you can look straight at me to answer the questions. Before the war, the area of Voljavica and the environs, was that a peaceful area?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain briefly for the Chamber when did you notice the situation changed?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. In that area, we started noticing things right after the cessation of Slovenia and particularly after the war broke out in Croatia, and then we noticed that the situation in that area started changing and that the Serbs started insisting on the thesis that their population was endangered, particularly in the areas where Muslims were in majority.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: By which means did they try to disseminate that idea of the Serbs being endangered?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: It usually went via the media, newspapers, the television.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: During 1990 and 1991, did you have any knowledge on the organisation and the activities of the SDS in that area?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was it that you noticed?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: We noticed that in the villages surrounding Voljavica, particularly in the village of Pobrdje, Miroslav Deronjic was a frequent guest there, and he was the local SDS representative from Bratunac and he used to meet with the people in Pobrdje.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice something that made you conclude that some arrangements of the SDS are being implemented in the field?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, they had already begun collecting volunteers to be sent to the war in Croatia to fight the Croatian Catholic population.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. How did you attain such information? How come you know of that personally? Did the Serbs try to cover up those departures to fight in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: No. They used to state it publicly. They didn't even try to hide it. They were proud of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. I would just like to ask the Trial Chamber to note that the Prosecution will not be making objections in terms of leading questions during what we consider this background period building up to things a bit more relevant to our indictment, but just to note that the witness is being asked about how did he reach conclusions and things of that nature which we haven't had a proper foundation, but seeing that we are with a lengthy witness that might take time, the Prosecution will allow some of the leading questions but we just would like to let the Trial Chamber understand that's the reason we are not at this point offering objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's pretty much in conformity with the practice that we are adopted so far. Thank you, Ms. Sellers. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was trying to get through this part of the testimony as quickly as possible in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: During 1991, that is the latter part of 1991, did you know of an event that related directly to the war in Croatia and pertaining to your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. area?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was it about?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: At that time, the Serbs had a propaganda show, so to say, in order to show how endangered they were in that area, and that was broadcast by the Belgrade television. They found several people who sold some of their property, much earlier, and they tried to portray those people as being expelled from that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you in possession of any information that some people from your area were being killed in Croatia? And did you know of some funerals?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any such funeral?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The particularly well known funeral is the funeral of a fighter from Zaluzje who was killed in the Croatian front.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was that just a regular funeral or was it something completely different?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: The Serbs made the best use of that funeral to promote their Chetnik insignia. They displayed the so-called cockades that they used to wear in the Second World War, and the Muslims have been injured greatly, in particular, by that insignia and the people who used to wear it then.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the area of Voljavica and the surrounding Muslim villages, were there any crimes committed at that time in the Second World War by the Chetniks, by the people who used to wear cockades?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. My grandfather was killed in the Second World War by the Chetniks, as well as a lot of other people from Voljavica. In this recent war, my father was killed by them, and it seems that it moves on from one generation to the next and it is always the same insignia.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that at the beginning of 1992, you became a member of the reserve forces of the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Performing those tasks, did you used to cover the area of Voljavica?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you move about in the wider area at that time when you were a reserve policeman at the beginning of 1992? Did you move about a wider area including the area of Bratunac and the villages associated with that municipality?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a member of the police reserve force, did you used to carry a semi-automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Performing the tasks of a reserve policeman, were you in position to acquire certain information and to have some knowledge about the events in the field starting from 1991 all the way to the beginning of the war in 1992?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you in contact with a lot of people, both Muslim and Serb, from your area?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Performing my duties, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Via those contacts, did you acquire some information?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you forward such information to anyone?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. To the public security station in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a reserve policeman, were you in a situation to be able to notice something pertaining to the activities of the SDS of that area?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: A minute ago you mentioned that you knew Mr. Miroslav Deronjic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please again tell the Chamber who Miroslav Deronjic was?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Miroslav Deronjic was the leader of the Bratunac SDS, their president.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned that he contacted two people, Nikola Ostojic and Branko Obrenovic. Could you tell the Chamber who those two people were?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those are people from our neighbouring village of Pobrdje and they were the local SDS representatives for their localities.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would kindly ask the usher to put a Defence Exhibit, D625, before the witness. This is a document of the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's a document of the Main Staff of the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it's called instruction on organising and the activities of organs of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina in extraordinary circumstances. This was issued in Sarajevo on the 19th of December, 1991. First of all, Witness, before you look at this document, I would like to ask you something. Is it true that the Bratunac municipality, before the war, was a municipality with a majority Muslim population, if we look at it overall?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a long document referring to the organisation and activities of the organs of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina in extraordinary circumstances, but I would like to ask you about things that you yourself were able to notice while working out in the field as a reserve police officer. Please, I would like to draw your attention to page -- do you have the document in front of you? Can you open it at page that has 2, the number 2 up in the corner, and that's the page that contains item 5 there. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to quote to you this item 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the English translation this is on page 3. Item 5 of the instructions of the SDS Main Board states: "Preparations are to be made for the formation of municipal state organs an executive board, administrative organs, magistrate's court, public security stations, et cetera, and proposals are to be made for personnel that will be holding the posts and carrying out duties in these organs. Preparations are to be made for taking over the staff facilities and equipment of security services, centres and their attachment to a newly established body for internal affairs at the centre headquarters." What I would like to ask you now is the following: Did you, in early 1992, notice anything specific in the behaviour of Serb police officers? We are talking about the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. In that period they no longer wanted to work together with us, to go on patrols, on mixed patrols, patrols of mixed composition.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at item 9 now, which is on page 3? Could you please find item 9? Could you please turn the page and find item 9 now? On the English -- in the English version it's on page 3. I'm going to read to you this item 9. Quoting: "Estimates are to be made of the necessary number of members of an active and reserve police structures of the TO, Territorial Defence, units and civil protection units. And in keeping with that, these structures are to be reinforced and all other necessary steps are to be taken for their activation according to how the situation develops." What I would like to ask you now is the following: Could you please comment on this part that refers to the reserve police forces? Did you notice --

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. At this time, the Serbs had many more cadres in the police reserve force, even though their settlements were much smaller than the Muslim settlements. For example, the village of Voljavica is much bigger than the village of Voljavica -- of Bjelovac, and we only had five reserve police officers there. While there were twice as many reserve police officers in Bjelovac. There were ten. And the situation was similar in other places in the Bratunac area.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any -- did you see anything in particular regarding the arming of the reserve police officers?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: The weapons that we were issued were mostly old weapons. I was issued a semi-automatic rifle. Very few Muslims received an automatic rifle. Most frequently it was the M48 which means that it was manufactured in 1948. While the Serbs mostly were issued with automatic weapons of more recent manufacture.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber how was it possible for something like that to happen? And to go on happening?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was very possible, because all the leading or the leadership cadre at the Bratunac MUP were of Serb ethnicity. There were some Muslims but not so many.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The chief of the SJB in Bratunac was Sead or Senad Hodzic. He was a Muslim. According to what you know, was he in a position to prevent this type of conduct, if you know?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do. He wasn't or he didn't have very much say in these matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to take you back to the document again. You were talking about propaganda activities. Could you please look on this same page, item 8 of the instruction of the Main Board of the SDS? This is also on page 3 of both the Bosnian and English versions. I will quote. "Information propaganda activities are to be intensified in order to inform the Serb people promptly and completely about the political and security situation in the municipality and further afield." Mr. Malagic, do you agree that in this period, from early 1992 up until the war, the propaganda information activities were intensified in relation to the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let us continue now with this document. Could you please look at item 11 of the instruction? It's on the same page that you were just looking at. I am quoting: "Preparations are to be made, organisational and other conditions created for the protection of children, pregnant women, elderly people, sick people, invalids or disabled people including preparation force protection and evacuation to less endangered areas in full cooperation with the commands and headquarters of our armed forces, (JNA)." So this is an instruction by the Serbian Democratic Party. Do you agree that the Serbian Democratic Party considered as its own the JNA forces?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was this actually demonstrated out in the field, in practice?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. We, the members of the police reserve forces, always knew when they were carrying out an evacuation of children, elderly women, the elderly, mostly to Serbia. All of this was covered by Radio Television Belgrade. Men of military age and younger women were the ones who mostly stayed at home.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Did you have information whether they were assisted in this by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, this part of the instruction by the SDS Main Board, which I just pointed out to you, was this implemented in Serbian villages in your area around Voljavica and in the Bratunac area?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was absolutely implemented.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Along with what was happening in the early months of 1992, did you notice if anybody around you was receiving weapons or being armed? The usher can now remove the document.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did notice.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any specific information about who was being armed in that area? Which people?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The population of Biljaca, Bjelovac. Most often Lasovac, constantly reported to us that they were seeing armed Serbs who were leaving in columns from Bjelovac towards Kunjarac in uniforms of olive-drab colour, and they were carrying out shooting practice and training there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said they reported to us, the citizens of certain villages reported to us. When you say, "Us," who do you mean? Are you thinking of yourself and somebody else most probably? Could you please explain that to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm thinking of us, members of the reserve forces of the police who were working in that area at the time. I can also give you their names.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Esad Alic, Samir Vlic, Munid Suljagic, Kadrija Jusic. They were my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned that they -- that people from Biljaca reported to you that they were seeing columns of armed and uniformed Serbs moving from the direction of Bjelovac towards Kunjarac and were undergoing training there, can you remember who was it who reported this to you?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Most often, this was reported to us by Sadif Zukic and many others.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have similar information for other regions as well? For example, for Pobrdje?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The citizens of Lasovac and the citizens of Voljavica who lived closer to Pobrdje constantly reported to us that they were also seeing large groups of armed and uniformed men who were leaving from Pobrdje through Tablja in the direction of Obadi.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you indicate this on the map?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Pobrdje, Tablja is not drawn in and then towards the Obadi road.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark with the letter T the settlement of Tablja because that is something that we will be mentioning during your testimony. Very well. Could you please tell us these things that the people reported to you, was this -- did this become more intense in a certain period? Did this intensify or not?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. In March, in mid-March, and in -- and early April, this was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. something that happened every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are you thinking of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You, a member of the police reserve forces, and other members of these police forces, in general Muslims, did you exchange information amongst yourselves, information that you received?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you inform the public security station in Bratunac about that?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was our duty to send reports to the station.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could the witness now be shown three documents? These are similar documents. They follow one another. These are Exhibits D101, D102 and D103.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please look at document D101? These are salaries for May 1992. It says Rakovac, the first company. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, first platoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Rakovac, first platoon, there is a large computer number 01320211. That's the page.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the list? I will draw your attention to certain persons. Could you please look at the name under number 7, Vujadin Prodanovic?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And then number 22, Dragan Prodanovic?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, could you please turn the page and then look where it says the second platoon, and if you can look at the names of the persons under number 2, Djordjo Djurkovic; 4, Dragojlo Neskovic; 15, Dusan Prodanovic; 25, Stevo Jakovljevic; number 32, Slavko Alempic, and now I would like you to turn to the next page and look at number 24, the name Goran Vasic, and I would like to ask you if you know any of these people?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know these people very well. They are from Rakovac, it's a neighbouring village next to Voljavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of March and April 1992, did you receive any information or any reports regarding these people or not?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. These people that you just -- whose names you just read out were all seen armed and uniformed. The citizens -- a citizen from the village of Voljavica who was transporting stones from the River Drina once reported that he encountered these people who were with weapons and uniforms and they were leaving towards the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you compile a report about this and send it to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was our duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please now look at this document again? And I would like to draw your attention to these markings next to the names. For example, under number 7, Vujadin Prodanovic, it says, PAP and so on and so forth. Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber what this means, PAP, M48, what you see in this document under the column that's titled "weapons"?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are abbreviations for infantry weapons from the ex-JNA. For example, PAP, means semi-automatic rifle. AP means automatic rifle. MP means machine-gun. Then another machine-gun, it's a 53, as it was called. So all these are abbreviations indicating artillery weapons which were used in the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When Mr. Sirucic [phoen] reported this event or incident, did he describe what these people whom we mentioned had, in terms of weapons?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at these names that we talked about? Did he mention these specific weapons?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. He did mention the weapons that are indicated here on this list.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. Did he tell you what -- or did he report to you what these people were wearing, what kind of clothing they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The majority of the people were wearing olive-drab uniforms, JNA uniforms. Some of them also had multi-coloured uniforms. It's probably something that was brought from the Croat front.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I would like to you look at D103. It's also a list of salaries for May 1992. The title of the document is, "List of soldiers of the MB 120 Squad." Do you have that document in front of you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the document. Under number 1, it says, Savo Lukic, Pobrdje?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then number 4, it states, Dragan Neskovic?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And then under number 15 it says Mico Gavric. Do you know these people?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Dragan Neskovic was a policeman before the war in Bratunac. Mico Gavric was the foreman at the Sase mine. He was actually my father's foreman and all of us from that area knew him.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to these people, in the second half of April 1992, did you receive any information?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the -- on the outskirts of Voljavica, the Bekric family lived. They were above Pobrdje and Tablja. I remember very well. He was very disturbed. He came to our checkpoint in Voljavica and said that there were mortars stationed at Tablja. He saw that very well. I mean he knew those weapons. He was evidently upset and he said that they were pointing towards Voljavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said Bekric. Do you remember the full name of that person?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Bekric, Selman.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk some more about that with him? Did he see any people there?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. He confirmed to me that Neskovic, Dragan was there, and Mico Gavric, and he was expecting the police to do something.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher now please show the witness document D102?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a list for payment of salaries for May 1992. It states here, list for payment of salaries for May 1992, and then in parentheses, it says various TOs. Could you please look at name under number 2, Simic, Zoran, Bjelovac; and then the number -- the name under number 7, Dragan Prodanovic, Rakovac. Do you know these people?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke about Prodanovic a little bit earlier. He was on that TO list in the Rakovac second platoon. And I knew Zoran Simic personally. He was from Bjelovac or Kunjarac more precisely. People from Bileca often said about him that he was an extremist, that he insulted the Muslim population in Bileca and Lasovac, that he was always in uniform, even in April, that they often saw him armed, that he threatened people and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did you personally, while you were working as a reserve police officer, have any contact with an arms shipment to the Serbs in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when this was and exactly what it was about? Could you please tell the Trial Chamber about it?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And just one moment, please. In April 1992. This event that you will tell the Trial Chamber about, is that something that you saw yourself, by yourself, or were there any other people with you and if you were in the company of other people, who were they?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: There were people from the reserve police forces, such as Esad Alic, Samir Vilic, and an active police officer, Mujo Husic. While we were on routine patrol on the road towards our football pitch in Voljavica, we noticed that from across the Drina, from Ljubovija, from the Brioni hotel there were some light signals being made with a flashlight, and shortly after that we noticed the same signals on the other side, the Bosnian side, in Pobrdje to be more precise, and we set off in the direction of those signals. As we were walking, we could see that there was a boat coming close from other side of the Drina. We couldn't see exactly how many people were there in the boat. We could see that there were some cases there. When we approached the light signals we could hear the voice, "Halt," and then there was a burst of fire. We threw ourselves on the ground. We were scared. We were shouting, "This is the MUP Bratunac police here. Don't shoot." We also perhaps fired one or two bullets in the air. We heard a voice from the other side, "Police officers, don't shoot. Kosta is here." Then we got up. We approached them. There was a man there standing from Pobrdje, that was Kosta Neskovic. He had his hands up in the air, "Don't shoot, brothers." He thought we were Serbs. He said, "Brother Serbs from Serbia are shipping weapons to us." However, when the shooting broke out, the boat returned to the other side, towards Serbia, and we brought Kosta into the Bratunac police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the way there, did you talk with Kosta? What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was slightly intoxicated. He said that there were more people there, the rest of them ran off, I don't know why. He said that they were cowards, and he said that they were constantly receiving weapons from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, according to your information, this statement of his about weapons, was that something that he provided in a statement to the Bratunac public security station?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, to Inspector Fehim. Because the next day they came out for an on-the-scene investigation, and they found shells of a certain type of weapon, Ruskie [phoen] Dobosar, that was used in the TO at the time. Drum cartridges.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like the witness to look at another document before the break. Could we please show the witness an excerpt from a book? It's a book, "The Truth about Bratunac," written by Nijaz Masic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to show you an excerpt on page 26. Could you please follow what I am reading very carefully, Mr. Malagic? This is written by Nijaz Masic and it's from his book, "Truth about Bratunac." And it states here: "Using the current situation after the murder in Kajici and the completed programme of evacuation of the Serbs from Bratunac municipality, the same day when Koljevic visited Kravica, the delivery of weapons to Serbs was organised by boats from Serbia over the River Drina. During the same night, after Koljevic left the village guard of Voljavica, local community, discovered the transfer of weapons from Ljubovija by boats on the section of the Drina River that lies below the Pobrdje village. On that occasion, the village guard arrested Kosta Neskovic from Pobrdje who was captured while securing the boat which was loaded with weapons. The arrested Neskovic was delivered to the public security station of Bratunac immediately. However, the village guard did not manage to seize the weapons because fire was opened from across the Drina from Ljubovija, from the Brioni area." I would like to ask you the following about this: This excerpt of Nijaz Masic's book, does that truthfully represent the event that you talked about?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: No, it does not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber when this incident in Kajici occurred and when did Mr. Nikola Koljevic visit that area, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. The murder of two Muslims in Kajici took place in September 1991. And this event on the Drina took place in April 1992. So it's considerably later than this other event, and these two events are not linked in any way at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Another thing: It states here that on the arrival of Koljevic, the village guard discovered the weapons shipment from Ljubovija. You participated in these events. Was this something that involved the village guard at all or was this something else?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: No. We were regular members of the public security station in Bratunac. We were the reserve forces and there was also an active police officer with us and we had instructions to carry out our duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We are still talking about this time period when this incident occurred. Did the Public Security Service in Bratunac still function jointly?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So this excerpt of Nijaz Masic's book, which talks about this whole incident, including the visit by Nikola Koljevic, the time period, as well as -- which mentions the village guard, is this incident true or not?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: No, it is not true at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we would like to have a number for this Defence exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Madam Vidovic. This document, which is being tendered in both the original language and in the English translation of it, consisting of the photocopy of the title of the book and of the publishing details, and page 26 of the original language, accompanied as stated by the corresponding English translation, is being marked as Defence Exhibit D758. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps this would be a good time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, according to what you knew then, did the Muslim population of the area know of the arming of the Serbs, speaking Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. generally?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, even the children knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did that cause fear and panic amongst the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The people of Lasovac were frightened in particular, as well as people in Biljaca and Bjelovac, because they knew that even at that time there were strong armed units in the Serb village of Bjelovac and Kunjarac in particular. They knew that there were about 100 armed people there, as well as at the Sase mine. As of March, the Serbs occupied an ammunition and explosives depot used for the mine and since then the regular workers stopped coming to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you learn of that personally from the local populace as a policeman?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did murders start taking place at a certain point?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The initial murders happened in the Bratunac municipality. I remember the first victim, a rather victims, these are the Skenderovic brothers, Emir, and his brother as well as their father. That murder was infamous for its brutality. They were not only murdered but they were also fixed with equipment used -- usually used for horses, that was attached to their bodies. That was particularly brutal.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember the period approximately when such murders started taking place?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Around the 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember what was happening with the police at that time?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: A policeman of Serb nationality simply established another police station in the old elementary school, Midhat Haca, in Bratunac and they took their weapons with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did they choose amongst themselves their chief, and who was it, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it well. It was Luka Bogdanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did they do anything in relation with the Muslim policemen?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They issued an ultimatum that all Muslim policemen turn over their weapons, so the Muslim policemen did in order to prevent an outbreak of a conflict, according to their chief's orders and his name was Senad Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you remember, did you speak with Senad Hodzic personally and if you did, did he ever explain his order that the Muslim policemen turn over their weapons?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did talk to him. He told us, "You should do the same. You should turn over your weapons. We want to avoid conflict. We will turn over our weapons and then we'll see what they wish to do next."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the Muslim policemen of Bratunac turned over their weapons? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. All of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did -- was the conflict avoided with the Serbs as was hoped for?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: No. Quite the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the Chamber what was happening in the next few days with the Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: I remember the murder of Sukrija Gusic and his underage son. Then came the attacks against the villages of Hranca.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please point it at the map?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: I don't see that on the map. Yes, there is Hranca, and Suha, Borkovac but Hranca and Borkovac were particularly under attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Provide brief answers and answer to my questions. Can you remember anything in particular concerning the attack on Hranca? Could you describe that for us and how did you come to know such information?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. My wife was from Hranca. She was 18 at that time. She was attending high school. And her father was executed in front of her. Her brother was beaten and taken to the Vuk Karadzic school and they attempted to rape her. They ripped off her clothes but only thanks to her mother, they didn't. She stood up to the attackers, and my wife managed to escape through the woods to Konjevic Polje, and the people there found her half-naked, and she was hysterical for a month, and for the next five years she knew nothing of her immediate family, and they didn't know what happened to her and she is still traumatised today.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened with the remainder of the population of Hranca at that day?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Some families were completely executed, like the Salkic and Ramic families. They were exhumed only last year. And they received a decent funeral then.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How about the rest of the population?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: In the village of Borkovac, I believe 35 people were executed. Only Hamidalic survived that and I believe he testified as to that before the Tribunal. Then the village of Suha. That was torched. A lot of people were killed, and those who survived fled towards Voljavica, Zaluzje and Biljaca. Some were taken to the Vuk Karadzic school while others were killed right there. Women were raped systematically and a group was taken to the Gradina camp at Sase and then their fate is unknown until last year when their bodies were exhumed from a mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned several mass executions, including the one in Borkovac. Could you tell the Chamber whether the people that were executed were armed or were they civilians? For example, Mr. Alic, can you remember who was executed alongside with him?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can. His wife Halima was killed. His father, who was an elderly person. Then a young girl by the name of Alma; I knew her well. And all of them were women and elderly, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the same fate befall Mihajlevici and Redzic?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, completely the same. The people who survived fled to Voljavica and Zaluzje.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You heard their stories personally as to what happened?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What happened in early May of 1992 in Glogova? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. In Glogova, next to the local mosque, 65 people were executed. Their bodies were found two years ago in a mass grave close to the mosque. The DNA identification was carried out, and they received a decent funeral and the place of their execution is marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What happened with the population that survived from those Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: They fled whichever way they could. They hid in the forests, some fled towards Bljecevo and Glogova, some towards Voljavica, and towards the villages that were up on the hill.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything of a certain part of that population that was taken to some camps?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. We learned that a lot of people were taken to the Gradina camp at Sase and some girls spent years literally at the Fontana at Bratunac. They were raped and abused, and we learned of that later at Likari via communication means.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I want to interrupt you. When you refer to this group of girls that was raped at the Fontana Hotel, I have a question regarding that. Do you know Edina Karic?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you referred to that group of girls, is that a group that she was a part of?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: No. That was not the same group. Edina was from Vlasovac and that was a separate group. And the other group I referred to included women from various areas like Suha, Mihajlevici, Glogova and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who had the Fontana Hotel under control at that time, the Serb or the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: There were no Muslims in Bratunac at the time. They were either expelled or killed. They went towards Tuzla and Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just a correction for the transcript. Witness, it is stated here that people from Glogova fled towards Glogova. I believe you said something different. Where did the people from Glogova flee to?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: They fled towards Bljecevo which is across the hill, towards Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I am reading the same line, that is -- was missing and I thank you for it, Ms. Vidovic and then it says also some towards Voljavica as well. I mean, perhaps he can confirm that because the direction to Srebrenica is one way, to Voljavica is another.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please clarify for the Chamber the movement of the population? What were the directions they took?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: People from Glogova fled towards Bljecevo, a majority of them, but several of them fled the other way, they didn't know that Mihajlevici and the villages alongside the Drina were torched. So -- and then they took the route towards Voljavica but via the Drina. They went through the fields.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Hence some of them reached Voljavica in the end. A further clarification, is Cizmici a part of Bljecevo?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's a small portion of Bljecevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge of the murders of Muslims in Bjelovac at the beginning of May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you briefly describe for the Chamber the situation?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: In the vicinity of Bjelovac, next to the Drina, there was a site where gravel was extracted, and two brothers of Muslim origin used to extract bodies that were floating in the Drina, and I remember clearly that Mujic Kiram was the first victim from Vlasovac, then Asim Redzic from Srebrenica. He was taken there and killed. And he used to be a football coach of the Guber team. Then Sahim [phoen], who was a police inspector, as well as numerous others who were buried unidentified, some were buried in Voljavica, for example, Redza [phoen], he was buried in Voljavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I have a follow-up question, then. In your knowledge, did the Serb population of Bjelovac know of these murders?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Some were even present when bodies were taken out of the river and the murders usually took place at night.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If a Serb inhabitant of Bjelovac would say that he didn't know of any murders or expulsions of Muslims in May of 1992, that is early May, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, prior to the witness answering the question, I would state that that question is not a question that he's capable, if a Serb did say that. I mean, there is a possibility a Serb did say that and he wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it doesn't make a difference. I mean, the question I think it is -- it's you know what the relevance of the question is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, certainly, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically it's being put to the witness that he needs to comment on what his conclusion would be as regards such an allegation or such a statement forthcoming from a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: In the hypothetical, I would imagine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course, he doesn't know who we are talking about. Obviously he probably would be in a position to answer better if he knew exactly who we are talking about because it does make a difference between someone who just makes a statement simply because he happens to be a Serb and someone who makes a statement who happens to be a Serb but also living in the area during the time in question, who should be in a position to know what happened and what did not. But anyway, let's move. I mean, I think we are there. I mean, if it's possible, Madam Vidovic will try and restrict her questions to what is basically relevant. I didn't stop you as regards all these killings because I knew where you were heading, but on the other hand, we don't need to protect it unduly. Already, please do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Just to the extent that relates to the credibility of the witnesses that testified as to this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know that, Ms. Vidovic. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain how come the people from the area, including the Serbs, knew of such information?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Every person that was killed had a last name. They lived in the same area. They knew each other. Kiram Mujic was the first victim, and he lived with his Serb neighbours. He was related to some of them and some of them even came to his funeral. They knew that information. People were living house to house. It couldn't be hidden.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To move on, can you remember what took place in the first half of May of 1992 in your village?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The local SDS representatives from Pobrdje invited our local commune representatives. They told them that weapons should be turned over, including hunting rifles held by the people in Voljavica, and the ultimatum stated the 11th of May for the handing over of the weapons and that they had to appear personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Our people, the elderly in particular, thought that our houses would be torched unless we did that. Perhaps some younger people would refuse but we knew what happened in Hranca and Glogova and Mihajlovici, but we obeyed what the elders said and some hunting rifles from turned over as well as a couple of guns that had licences.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you turn in your own weapon?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I turned over my semi-automatic rifle that I was given by the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did anything take place on the 12th of May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. If you have Voljavica in mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Right after the weapons were turned over, people started leaving Voljavica en masse, moving towards Poloznik and Pirici. Voljavica is a rather big place. Some people who still trusted Serbs, who worked with them or were related to them, remained. But most of the people moved towards other localities. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your father, did he remain in the village or did he leave the area?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: We had a large number of cattle there at that time and he remained behind to feed them. The rest of the family left the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you personally go?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: I left with my mother and my brothers to Poloznik.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you learn from anyone as to what happened in your village on that day?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I learned that from my parent, from my father, who told me that on the 12th of May, Voljavica was attacked from all directions, from Pobrdje, from Tablja, and right on the spot, Avdo Ahmici was killed as well as Sabet Sjosic [phoen]. He told me that the population was taken to the bus station, put on buses that took them to Tuzla and Kladanj. A part of the inhabitants managed to hide away, including my father, next to a water utility facility, and they observed it all, and in three days later they reached us and then at the they told us the story.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did your father tell you who attacked Voljavica? Were those people from afar or did he know them?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: My father told me very emotionally what happened. He recognised many of the attackers, and other people who were telling me that story were telling me the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What did he say? Where did those people come from?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: He recognised a lot of them, and he mainly said that those were our neighbours from Pobrdje, Bjelovac and Sase.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you that the attack was organised or anything in that sense?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. He said that they had commanders who issued directions, who were familiar with Voljavica and they told them which directions to take.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did he mention anyone in specific?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was very surprised to see Slavoljub Rankic, aka Slavko. He knew him well, as well as his father, Nedjo. They passed by close to him with a group of people issuing orders. He told me that in that group, there was Krsto Rankic as well. And he knew all of them very well. Then Slavoljub Filipovic, all from Bjelovac. He mentioned some people from Pobrdje, Sreten Ilic, Golub Lukic. I knew those people as well. Then Radomir Ostojic, who was right -- who lived next to Voljavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could we please now show D83 to the witness? It is a list of the Bjelovac TO, salaries paid for June of 1992. Witness, please take a look at some names. Please turn to the third page and the number is 01335441. At the top, it says, TO Bjelovac. Please look at number 571, and the name there. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Krsto Rankic. Then 572, Slavko N. Rankic?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: 584, Slavoljub D. Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are these the people that your father mentioned to you as participants of the attack?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. He knew all of them and, if I may add, he said that Krsto was very intoxicated and that he kept asking Slavko to let him join the Bule and that was the name he used for the Muslim women.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Slavko Rankic, does that person have some other name or is this a short name?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: His full name is Slavoljub Rankic but everyone called him Slavko.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Apart from the conversation you had with your father, did you discuss this issue of the attackers against Voljavica with some other people from Voljavica?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke with my uncle, who is an elderly person, as well as Camil Mehmedovic and many others. They all confirmed the same story because they knew these Serbs from before.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you what they -- who they thought commanded the attack?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: They all kept mentioning Slavko Rankic as the commander or the leader of the attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to put another document before the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a new document, the number is 01335456, TO Pobrdje, salaries for June of 1992. The number is 01335456. Witness, please take a look at this document. Please go to the page that starts with TO Pobrdje and take a look at the number 1382. Radomir Ostojic; can you see that?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then number 1371, Sreten Ilic?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: 1375, Golub Lukic. Are those the people your father mentioned as the attackers in Voljavica on the 12th of May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are precisely the people and he knew them very well, and I know them because they were our neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please give this document an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Madam Vidovic. Let me just ask a couple of questions before I do. It will of course become Defence Exhibit D759. But in order to be precise for the record, I see that the first page as ERN number 01335404 and that is the front page of this document. I'm referring to the original language, B/C/S. Then the next page is 01335456. Then that page is followed by 01335457. Then I have a next page which at least in the photocopy, and this is why I am putting a question to you, in the photocopy that I have for the next page, and the one following, I do not have an ERN number. I would take it that the first of these is -- ends with 5458 and 5459 because the page immediately following does have an ERN number and would complete the sequence as it is 5460. So if you confirm to us that these two pages where we have the photocopy without an ERN number are indeed pages with -- ending in 5458 and 5459, we can confirm that for the record. It's probably a problem of photocopying more than anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I can confirm that. It happens when we are printing that the number cannot be seen or you can only see half the number. However, as you can see here, the numbers that follow when you look at the order of the people, then it's clear, whereas the first column during printing is also missing one number, and a part of the next number. But this is something that is really beyond our influence because we -- it was printed and then we copied what we received. These are large documents, for example, and they are entitled personal salary for June 1992, and then there is a large group of units of the Bratunac Brigade. We only take just the relevant parts. Otherwise we would have to be providing you with very, very large documents, and then the numbers actually go the way you mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand. I just wanted a confirmation that those two pages which do not show an ERN number are indeed 5458 and 5459 and I think I'm satisfied, at least -- Judge Eser, are you satisfied too? That we are satisfied that it is so. So let's describe this new exhibit. In the original language it consists of six pages. The first one ending in -- having ERN number 01335404, followed by five pages starting with 01335456 and ending in 5460, accompanied by three pages in English purporting to be translation of the original documents. The totality is being tendered in evidence and marked as Defence Exhibit D759. The corresponding English part would have an E at the end. Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please tell the Trial Chamber what happened with the population, the Muslim population, that was expelled from the villages that you mentioned, including Voljavica, after these events in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The expelled population was together in columns and they sought shelter around the villages of Poloznik, Pirici and Lokva.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the Muslim population from Lasovac, Gradina and Sase went?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had -- they were together in a large column of people in Loznik, in Bare, to be more precise. That's what that place was called.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And how many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: There were thousands of them there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And where did the expelled population of Voljavica, Zaluzje and Biljaca concentrate?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: These citizens got together in columns and went near the village of Podloznik or at the location of Ljuljaska to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How many people were there in that column?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: That was the largest group of people in that area, because these were large Muslim villages. It was terrible to see those groups of people in camps.
