They found it very hard to believe that they could get killed just because they were Muslims, that their houses could be burned, that they could be left with no property overnight. They had with them only those things that they had taken with them from their homes. They were afraid. They had small children. There was no water. They slept in the open air and it was still cold in May there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How many of them were there at Ljuljaska?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: You couldn't establish the exact number but it was approximately up to 2.000 people. There were smaller such refugee camps also. There was one in the area of the village of Pirici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And these groups of people, you described that they lived in very difficult conditions, did they have any houses where they could take shelter?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: No. These were makeshift camps with housing made from trees, branches, pieces of plastic, they spread leaves on the ground. It was hard to conceive this in the 20th century that rich people would have to leave their homes and then would be reduced to such living conditions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Besides the fact that they were living in such conditions and in very difficult material conditions, were they able to live at least peacefully, even though they were in such dire straits?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: No. Immediately in May, these makeshift camps were shelled intensely from Serb positions at Kunjarac, Jovanovici, and Sase. These were powerful mortar shellings, and people did not have peace because of this shelling. They even had to shelter small children in makeshift trenches in order to protect themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether you yourself personally knew -- you mentioned these locations but what I want to ask you is the following: How do you know that these makeshift camps were shelled from Kunjarac, Sase, these places that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: I know this very well. We went to the village of Bojeca [phoen] very often with some other men, and we saw Bjelovac and we could see where the smoke was coming from. We had an old set of hunting binoculars so we were able to observe that through that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And these people, were they civilians, were they soldiers in these makeshift camps?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: They were all civilians. We didn't have an army.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At some point, did a group of people form which managed to get their hands on some weapons at some point? Now I'm talking about the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Us younger people felt that it was necessary to protect these people from Voljavica, Bileca, Zaluzje, because there was a Serb incursion into this makeshift camp where the Vlasovac citizens were, and there was a massacre there. We had some hunting weapons and we received some weapons from the Podloznik citizens because they joined us, so we kind of made a line in front of our makeshift camp at Ljuljaska.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At one point, did you leave that area?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was hunger, the conditions were terrible. We found out from some people from Stozerska that Srebrenica was liberated and that perhaps the conditions, the living conditions, were better over there, so we set off through Podloznik, Lokva, Petinici, Predola, Dimnici, Skenderovici, Pribicevac towards Srebrenica, and a group of our people went with us, who were in these makeshift camps. It was not possible to stay in these camps any longer, so those who were braver amongst them came with us and we set out in the direction of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Skenderovici. Did you go through that location or did you bypass it?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Skenderovici was a Muslim settlement but we had to pass by the village of Pribicevac which was inhabited by Serbs. The pen is not working. Where the Serbs were living. And that is where we were attacked. We noticed --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, Witness. You will get a fresh pen.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: I'm going to mark Pribicevac. This is where we were noticed because it was a fairly large column. We were attacked. There were wounded people. The trip took us all day because we went through the woods, along creeks, and finally we managed to reach the Srebrenica area above Crni Guber and to go down to Srebrenica itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived at Srebrenica, do you remember what you saw there?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were all disappointed. We thought we would see what we knew about Srebrenica before. However, Srebrenica was burned. The mosques were demolished. It was a ghost town. You would see the odd inhabitant wandering around. It was a catastrophic defeat for us, what we saw in that town.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just tell us, do you remember when this was, what time, which month?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: It was mid-June, 1992. I'm speaking about 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At one point, you mentioned that a group of young people was armed --

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: No, the whole group did not leave. There was a group of men who formed the group at Pirici and they believed that they would be closer to Biljaca. They stayed with Sadif Zukic. He was their leader. We set off. We had our own leader, Osman Malagic. We set out towards Srebrenica. And Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. then from there we went to Likari.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At one point, when you came to Srebrenica, did you find out about a group of your people from Voljavica somewhere near Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a young man who was in Hakija Meholjic's group in Srebrenica and we found out at Likari, it's a village above Potocari, there were some people from Voljavica who had managed to get to Srebrenica earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And did you then go to Likari?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: We weren't thinking for too long. We went to Likari right away. We thought when we get there we would be closer to Voljavica and in that way we would be able to take food from our houses and food stores. Voljavica was a rich village so we had a lot of agricultural products there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you got to Likari, what was the situation that you found there? What I want to ask you actually is the following, where Likari, was Likari what inhabited place before the war?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, Likari was a small but very nice settlement, very pretty. When we got there, only two houses were intact. All the others were burned.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war, was Likari a Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Only Muslims lived in Likari.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you got there, were there any citizens there from Likari that you saw there?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Very few. When we got there, we found people who had fled from Potcaus while the inhabitants of Likari actually, the ones who survived the attack on Likari had escaped towards Pecista, Gosti [phoen] and Potocari in order to save themselves. I remember that they told us that Serbs captured four women at that time, that they kept at Likari all the time and they were systematically raped there, those four women.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just one moment. Let me ask you this. Now you're talking about four raped women but what I want to ask you is: Did you find out who attacked the village and when? When was the village of Likari burned, attacked and now you're talking about rapes? Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: We knew about it. The inhabitants told us from Obadi and Likari that they were attacked by Serbs from Obadi and Serbs from Zalazje because these were villages near Likari.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you properly, you came to Likari in mid-June 1992 with a group of people. Did your group have anyone that was leading it?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Our leader was Osman Malagic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you got there, did you encounter this other group of people and who led that group?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. When we arrived, the first thing was we were disappointed. We had come to the worst possible place and the most difficult line at the time in Srebrenica, and we met a small group of people from Potcaus and this group was led by a certain Naser Sabanovic. I remember the name well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Why do you say that you came to the worst possible line in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: We understood that Likari was a location or an elevation that was very important to the Serbs but it was also important to our inhabitants from Potocari, Gosti, and Pecista that they -- had they captured Likari, none of those people could be living in those villages because that was the highest elevation and they could fire at them. As long as they had that elevation every house in Potocari was hit by at least ten times [as interpreted] with artillery weapons. That is why that location was very important and it was also constantly under attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you talked about two different groups, a group led by Osman Malagic and another group led by Naser Sabanovic. Did these groups unite at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. We joined together and we guarded Likari together.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who decided to join these two groups? Did you do that or did some outside order come to this effect?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: We joined together by ourselves. We knew each other. Some people knew one another. We didn't need anybody to tell us. We joined together on our own. And Naser Sabanovic remained to be the leader for the whole of Likari because they had come earlier and they knew the terrain better than we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether in the second half of June of 1992 there were attacks on Likari? And where did these attacks come from?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: There were daily attacks on Likari. That is a story in itself. Most frequently, the attacks would come from the direction of Obadi, Zalazje and Sase.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that the attacks came from Sase?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: If you look on the map, you will see that Likari is on a large plateau above those places and that you have a good of the view of the roads towards Zalazje, Obadi, and you can also see Sase spread out below.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That group that you were in, what kind of weapons did it have and how many weapons?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Our group and this group were Potcaus had about 25 rifles altogether, old hunting rifles -- weapons, some of the old M48s, and that was it. We had very, very few weapons for such a dangerous region.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any assistance in ammunition, weapons and so on from anyone up until early July 1992?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: No. We never received any assistance in food or ammunition or weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether or not in early July 1992 there were any particularly intense attacks on Likari?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember the 2nd of July, I get always very emotional when I talk about that attack. I almost died. Likari almost fell that time. I remember that attack very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any assistance from anywhere on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the last minute, a group of fighters arrived from Potocari, and it was only with their help that we managed to defend Likari. We didn't have any more ammunition. I recall that I only had two bullets left for my M48 repeat action rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember any people who were in that group of people from Potocari?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that Naser Oric was in that group of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Other than this group from Potocari, did any other people come there?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since the attack lasted all day, a group from Srebrenica came to help us. I remember that this group was led by Becir Bogilovic, a police officer from Srebrenica. He was wounded in that attack. I remember very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And how was Naser Oric introduced to you or presented to you at that time?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Naser did not introduce himself to us at Omerovic. We saw him with a group of people from Potocari. In the course of the attack. He was with them, amongst them, in front of them, a fighter like any other fighter who was in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned this group of people that had arrived from Srebrenica. Was it your impression that Oric was commanding in any way, that he was in charge of that group of people that came with Becir Bogilovic as well?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: No. He didn't command anyone. Everybody had their own group. We were under the command of Osman Malagic. Becir had his own group. Naser's group was brought from Potocari. There was no coordination at all, once the attack started, you would look to find the best possible shelter.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And during this battle, did Oric coordinate the group? Did he issue any instructions, orders or anything like that? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: That was one of the fiercest battles. Nobody issued any instructions at all. When a bullet made a parting in my hair, I was the one who decided where I would hide. Had there been a mouse hole and there were shells, I would have fled there. This is the time when personal courage is demonstrated. Nobody listened to anyone else once the attack really started and got underway.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I understood that you did manage to defend Likari on that occasion. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After that, did you have an opportunity to speak with Oric and, if you did, did he explain why he had come there?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: After the battle, all the fighters got together. There were dead. We were discussing who had been killed, who had been wounded, and I remember that Naser said that they had heard a powerful or loud shooting and shelling in Potocari. I mean, you can hear that and they understood that Likari would fall and that is why they came to help us.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, did you, in Likari, and these people that you saw there, did you have uniforms?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: No. I was wearing jeans and a reserve police forces jacket, and we had civilian clothing, a shirt and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you one more question about Oric. At any point in time, do you remember seeing Oric ordering Osman or Becir or issuing instructions to them?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: No. He didn't issue orders to anyone. After the attack, they simply returned to Potocari, Becir returned to Srebrenica, and we stayed at Likari. So nobody issued any orders to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now we are talking about July 1992. Did you hear that in May 1992 there was a meeting of some kind in Bajramovici, where a staff was elected to be in command of all the armed forces in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: No, I never heard of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just ask that some caution be exercised because these are issues quite relevant to the indictment, to the case. And I do believe that we do have an amount of leading here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree 100 per cent with you, Ms. Sellers. In any case, the witness has answered that he's not aware of such a meeting. So ... Yes, Madam Vidovic, please your discretion. You don't need lecturing from me. Certain questions when it comes to pivotal matters, try not to lead. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in order to get a negative response or to get a response, I had to ask this question but I will rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, before you talked with me, did you ever hear about a meeting in Bajramovici before?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: No, never. This is the first time that I'm hearing about it. I don't know anything about a meeting in Bajramovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you very close to Osman Malagic?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was one of his closest associates. He was also my cousin. I was amongst the people who were very close to Osman Malagic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did he ever mention a meeting in Bajramovici to you?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: No, never. Had he known about it, I would have known about it for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: From your testimony, I understood that until mid-June 1992, you were in Pirici, in the Pirici and Podloznik region?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is this true?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In that period, did you ever hear from those people there mention Bajramovici in the context of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: No, I never heard anything like that. The most important thing for us was to survive and to find food.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you something about the groups of people you mentioned. The group at Pirici and the group you mentioned as headed by Osman Malagic, and the group brought along with Naser. What did you used to call them, those groups? Did you use military terminology? Designations of establishment? In that period in July of 1992 and for the rest of 1992, what did you used to call those groups?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: People who stayed in Srebrenica, we called them Hakija's men or Akif's men. The people from Potocari, Naser's men. We were called Osman's guys. We were all young. Or the people of Osmace, of Podloznik and so on and so forth. No military terminology was used.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: To move on to a different topic, how long did you stay at Likari personally?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Until the 14th of December of 1992, to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: During that period, did your group have any contact with Oric's group from Potocari?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: No. Just in case of fierce attacks. They would come to our aid. Otherwise, there were no other contacts.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Between July of 1992 and December 1992, did that happen on one or two occasions or more often, if you could tell the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: There were several strong attacks against Likari and people had to come at least five or six times, otherwise we would not have been able to defend it ourselves. And other people came as well, not only from Potocari but from Kazani, for example. They all knew we needed help.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was the role of Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just to try and understand better, Kazani, where is it exactly? I don't think it has been marked already on the map. If the witness can show it to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Kazani is here on the outskirts of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you just write the name of Kazani, if it's not there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is there. It's very small print. Barely visible. But it is there. Judge Eser would like to put -- sorry, Madam Vidovic. Judge Eser would like to put a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I just have an additional question with regard to Likari. Likari is written here in the map in a way that it seems to indicate a mountain region, was there a special place in Likari where you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were stationed? Because on the map it's not possible to identify the location of Likari. Could you perhaps clarify a little bit where you have been stationed with your group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Likari is on a plateau. You can see here these are the houses marking the settlement. We were located towards Obadi. There were lines around the houses because we spent our time in the houses, and we were at the Zanik hill as well. That's where our positions were. And Likari was then behind our back. And that's where we would spend the night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Zanik is also shown on the map, making it -- if you can mark it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will circle it again. Zanik is the highest hill in the Likari region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before I hand you back to Madam Vidovic, you've described Likari as situated on a plateau. Is there a town or a village which is also in the area and on this plateau that is known by the name of Likari? Or is it just the area that is referred to as Likari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There was a settlement by the name of Likari of about 20 houses. During the attacks of May, they were torched. Only two houses remained intact, which we could use to spend our time in. It used to be a very pretty place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this is why I'm asking you because you described it already as a very pretty place. And if you look at the map, Mr. Malagic, just beneath the L and the I, the first two letters of Likari, there is a tiny circle there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would that indicate this small hamlet of a few houses which was referred to by the name of Likari? Or would it indicate something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We have the same thing in mind. The small circle that you indicated is blue. This is Knjesavica [phoen], a river that flows through Potocari. The settlement of Likari is up above, close to A. You can see a few houses there, the black spots.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Madam Vidovic, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just to clarify something with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Judge Eser asked the following question: Where were you accommodated in Likari? And I wanted to ask you the following: Did you have accommodation? Did you have disposition in your lines or did you go there by yourselves?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: I said earlier that we went from Srebrenica to Likari by ourselves. Nobody told us, Go up there and keep the line. You can see where Voljavica is or where Likari is. We thought that we could go through the woods to reach Voljavica to get some food out.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Another question concerning this topic, the group you met there, did anyone put that group there in your knowledge or were they self-organised?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: That group was from Potcaus which was a hill up above Bratunac. When they were attacked, the closest settlement to them was Likari, and that's where they found some shelter.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Oric came to that area on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was his behaviour like during those attacks? To ask you again, was he issuing instructions? What was he behaving like?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: He was ahead [Realtime transcript read in error "a head"] of his people from Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I wanted to stop before the witness completed the answer, and that would be an example that I say is getting too close to leading, what was his behaviour like, was he ordering. Let the witness answer what was his behaviour like, let's not suggest it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Madam Sellers. Doesn't really make much difference in my opinion. I mean, I don't see much difference between the question as asked and your suggestion, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I explained already, when I was describing the attack of the 2nd of July, every time they came, Naser was ahead of them. Otherwise there were no instructions. Those were heavy shellings and everyone tried to find the best shelter. People were being killed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any logistical support from the people of Potocari?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: They didn't have any support and we didn't expect anyone to give us anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: To move on to a different topic, between July of 1992 and further, did you have any knowledge as to what was happening with the Muslim population of Voljavica, Zaluzje, Biljaca and other Muslim villages in the area?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had quite a lot of knowledge because the families of some of our men stayed in the area of -- and Podloznik with the refugees, and we know what they were going through, that they were short of food and that the conditions were very bad.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 13, the transcript states that the witness said that he was ahead of his people in Potocari but the witness meant something different. He meant ahead in the -- in combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could the witness please clarify?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Each of our leaders, including Naser for his Potocari group and Osman Malagic, who was the leader of our group, was in front of us. Otherwise they couldn't be the leader. So Naser was in front of his Potocari people. Osman was in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What does that mean? He was fighting in front of us?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. His behaviour was important for other fighters to see.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I do not mean to interrupt you, Mr. Malagic, but I would just like the witness to answer the question without a suggestion following what does it mean that he was ahead so we could be enlightened by your answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At this stage, you are encountering opposition --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Malagic, one moment. Madam Vidovic, we try to stick to the practice that we have adopted, that as long as you don't encounter opposition from the Prosecution, you can fire leading questions. When you do encounter opposition, let's stick to the normal rules of -- on not -- not resorting to leading question or making suggestion to the witness. I leave this entirely in your hands. And, Ms. Sellers, whenever you wish to object to the way a question is being put to the witness, please draw our attention and we'll decide accordingly. All right. I think the rules -- we know what the rules of the game, if I can call them that, are. As far as this trial goes. And let's try and stick to them. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I may just say one thing. One is just that with that -- the last correction, because in English you have a head of the people and ahead --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's why the clarification. As for leading, I did wonder whether at least the practice was followed that if you need to elicit a denial that you're allowed to put a leading question. So that if it's the case the Prosecution that Oric was issuing orders one of course can say was he issuing orders, otherwise there is no way to get the denial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I certainly did not mean to exclude such questions being put. We are used to the same procedure, you and I.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it's -- the other part, the transcript, yes, it says, a head, it says, if there is an article and a noun but I had understood it as being ahead meaning in front of. That's how I understood it. In fact, I don't watch the transcript all the time as we go along because I have other responsibilities like watching everyone else in the courtroom. So please, when there is something like that, do draw our attention because sometimes it is important and we need to take notice of it. Thanks. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you described the suffering of the Muslim population of the area. Does the word Predola mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Predola is a place where Muslims used to live. It had an elementary school with only two classrooms. A lot of refugees assembled there, refugees from our region. And in the classrooms there were usually children. They spent the night there whilst adults were slope outside. They had some water there as well. They could use it for washing or cooking.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: These refugee camps and groups in Predola itself, did such a situation continue until the 14th of September of 1992, that is in winter conditions as well?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The situation persisted until the 14th of December. For all those months people slept outside in makeshift camps without food or any conditions [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber what the consequences were for those people?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Catastrophic. They were sick often. There was no medical attention. The elderly could not survive that. Most of them died. Then the rains came and occasionally some of the local inhabitants would take them in until the rain would stop. And then there was no food. People tried to reach their previous settlements to get some.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you see the Muslims moving about the area in search of food?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. We saw that on a daily basis. They moved below Likari through the woods towards Voljavica, Zaluzje, and they would bring back corn and whatever they could find.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Concerning this, I wanted to ask you the following: Was there something unusual at that time to see a line, a column of 1.000 people searching for food in that area?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: No. It was a regular sight that we saw daily. We saw their suffering. It was a very difficult route to travel and they didn't know who would survive it and who wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask the usher to put a new document before the witness. This is a document by the command of the eastern Bosnian corps of the 28th of July of 1992. Active effect, order to all units. Quoting: "The order was issued by commander Colonel Dragutin Ilic on the 28th of July." Quoting: "All units are to set up ambushes on a daily basis and to have incursions in -- among enemy lines and to introduce sabotage groups in order to inflict casualties and cut off communication of enemy movement. And daily reports, the tasks carried out should be reported. All units within their zones should conduct cutting off of all enemy communications." Mr. Malagic, it is stated here on the 28th of July that enemy lines or communications should be broken. Do you remember that area or that period? What was really taking place?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: During that time, our people, who -- that went in search of food constantly came on ambushes. There were people being killed and wounded or captured. We tried to warn them but one couldn't stop a hungry person looking for food.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Hence this pattern of ambushes. Was it widespread in the area that you are mentioning?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was very widespread and I can give you the names of people who disappeared because of these ambushes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to ask you the following. In July of 1992, did you know of the existence of the east Bosnian corps? Could you please responds with yes or no?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you remember, when you came to Likari, did you find an apparatus there?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, an old radio station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, thank you. Could we please give it an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, before we move to something else, this document which consists of two pages, one in the original language, having ERN number 0438203 -- says if it's O and the corresponding translation into English is being tendered and received as a Defence Exhibit and marked as Defence Exhibit D760. Yes. Sorry for interrupting you. The question to you, Mr. Malagic, was if you remember when you arrived in Likari whether you found an apparatus there, and you answered -- or you had just started giving your answer by saying, yes, an old radio station. As it is -- as it shows in the transcript. I don't know if it was a station or whether it was just a radio transmitter. Perhaps you can explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He said a radio device.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you describe specifically the device?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: When we came to Likari we were shown this by the people who came there before us. I believe they brought it from Srebrenica, from the police station. It was broken. It could receive but couldn't transmit. So they used it to listen in on conversations of the local Serb units in that area of Likari. That's how we learned of the eastern Bosnian corps because it had frequent contact with the garrison in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally spend some time next to the device?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, often. Whenever I was not in the trenches I was present there because it was interesting to listen to the conversations.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you in a situation to overhear some data pertaining to Serb formations, apart from the eastern Bosnian corps?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were listening to the communication of the local units Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. from Andrici, Pobrdje, Bjelovac, Kunjarac. They discussed issues openly because they thought we couldn't hear. They didn't use any encryption, and we always listened to their conversations.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the device have several channels?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, it had several frequencies. Some of the frequencies used in encryption, we couldn't understand that but as for the other channels that we could hear, we could listen to their daily contacts from their positions, Bjelovac, Kunjarac, Pobrdje and Sase. That's what we overheard.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am about to move to a different topic, and if we may have a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, before we do. I thank you for that. Perhaps he can explain two things on this subject. Are you in a position, considering your training in the army, to tell us what was the make of the radio and the model? That's number one. And secondly, how was it powered at this time? These are the two questions that I have for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was made by Iskra which used to be a Slovenian company in the former Yugoslavia, usually used by the police administration to communicate with their patrols. As for the battery, we had an old car battery that soon died out and then some of the people remembered to create mini-generator plants using the flow of the water. We used an electrical engine. And the wheel was moved by the stream creating enough electricity to make the device work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The Prosecution would like to bring up an issue related to some of the recent motion filings. We would probably need more than three or four minutes in private session. I just ask the Trial Chamber whether they would like to do that at the close of today's session so that Madam Vidovic could continue as opposed to the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I would suggest that we leave everything until the end. Also I need about one minute, maximum two minutes, to provide on a matter that we discussed in closed -- in private session this morning, just a temporary order pending the outcome of what we are expecting. Yes, so let's finish ten minutes before quarter to 2.00, and then we will use the last few minutes to deal with these matters, all right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, we talked about the device and we also talked about whether you had heard any communications regarding Serb formations. Do you remember such communications coming through that device?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember well. They communicated often from Pobrdje and the communication was between Dragolub Lukic, Dragan Ilic from Bjelovac. We often heard communications between Sreten Petrovic. He would report from Spat first. And then also from Sase. Those are the communications that I remember best because they were of interest particularly to us in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like the usher to show the witness a new document. It's a document 004358251. A document by the Bratunac garrison command dated 12 October 1992. The document is called decision on appointment. I would like to read it to the witness: "I hereby appoint Dragan, son of Ivko, Ilic as commander of the first platoon of the Bjelovac company." So the Bratunac garrison command is appointing Ivko Ilic as commander of the first platoon of the Bjelovac company and asks that the order be executed immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please look at this document and tell us whether Dragan Ilic was a person whose communications you had heard with Dragolub Lukic? Did you know Dragan Ilic at all?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure that it's the same person because at one time we heard Dragolub Lukic congratulating him on the appointment through this radio communication, and I knew Dragan Ilic slightly. I knew his father much better. His father was a bus driver on the route that we travelled on quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And on what basis did you conclude that it was Dragan Ilic who was being talked about?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Dragan Lukic congratulated him, this command appointment, when they were talking. They were not trying to conceal their names at all. Dragan, Dragolub, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was there anybody around you who knew him better?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was Juso Cvrk from our group who used to go to school with Dragan, and he -- we always called him to listen when he was talking. He liked to listen to Dragan when he was talking.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could this document be given an exhibit number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This document, which consists of two pages, one in Serbo-Croat and the other one purportedly the English translation thereof, is being tendered and received as Defence Exhibit number D761. The Trial Chamber, however, points out that while on the B/C/S version the ERN number is 04358251, at the left bottom section of the English translation, the ERN number is erroneously indicated as being -- as ending with the four digits 9251. And then there is another four -- there are another four numbers, 9118/HMH. This anyway is document 761, D761. We don't need to bother any further with the discrepancy that there is. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I would now like you to look at a new document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please show the witness a new document? It's a document of the Bratunac garrison command, dated the 14th of August 1992, bearing the number 04358235. It's also an order. The Bratunac garrison command, on the 14th of August 1992, states the following: The -- I'm ordering the Bjelovac company to hold the positions in Bjelovac every day, organise a duty team by day and by night on the bridge in Bjelovac and secure the road towards Kunjarac as well as the bunker at the crossroads to Kunjarac and Kovacevici. The commander of the Bjelovac TO company and the platoon commanders are responsible for carrying out this task.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please comment on this document? Do the contents of this document mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The contents mean a lot. While listening in to their communications, we knew about this problem that they had. They were frequently criticised by the garrison command because they were not holding the bridge in Bjelovac as well as this bunker that was important to them and that was on the road towards Kunjarac. Later they captured the bunker but it was important to our people who were going towards Biljaca for the food because it was controlling this road along which people had to pass.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could this document be given an exhibit number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This document, which consists of two pages, the original in Serbo-Croat, bearing ERN number 04358235, the corresponding translation into English being the second page being tendered as Defence Exhibit and marked D762.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could the witness please be shown the next document? That's document -- another document by the Bratunac garrison command dated 11th of October, 1992. It states: Based on necessity and with the aim of performing combat activities and implementing the planned tasks, I order, item 1, carry out preparations to lift the Tomica hill, Andrici. Units to be activated are the Pobrdje company, the Red Beret Platoon and the Sase detachment. Persons responsible for implementing this task is first class captain Jovan Zivanovic." Could you please look at item 2 as well, which says: "To perform blocking of the Kunjerac-Kostanovice-Andrici line, units which should be activated are the Mostanice company 1, Kostanovice first platoon and Andrici platoon. Responsible persons for fulfilling this task are Angel Andjelko Obrenovic and Sreten Petrovic. I would now like to ask you also about the communications that you monitored over the radio device. In October, at this time, in mid-October 1992, did you know of the existence of the Pobrdje company, the Red Beret platoon, and the Sase detachment.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. We knew about the formations that existed at those locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How did you know this?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: We knew about that based on their communications. And also during our reconnaissance activities, we could see from neighbouring elevations where the mortars were located at Sase, Andrici and all of these other locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please pay particular attention to item 2 of this order, which states: "To carry out the blocking of the Kunjerac-Kostanovice-Andrici line, the units which should be activated as Mostanice company, Kostanovice first platoon and Andrici platoon. The responsible persons for fulfilling this task are Andjelko Obrenovic and Sreten Petrovic." Is Sreten Petrovic the person you said was calling from Sase?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He very frequently was the one who was calling from Sase.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And in relation to this I want to ask you the following: Is there any information or do you have any information or not whether in October 1992 the Kunjerac-Kostanovice-Andrici line was actually closed?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. In that period, they did manage to close that line.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please show this to the Trial Chamber, if you have the map in front of you?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Kunjarac was not put here on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether this is not part of Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is it a hill above Bjelovac. The line cut the road from Kostanovice and Andrici. Andrici is not here, but it's between Obadi and Kostanovice, so that complete line was closed. And it made it more difficult for our civilians to get food, especially to go -- going from the villages which were going down to Biljaca. They couldn't approach that area and also a stronger ring was placed around Likari.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could this document be given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So this document, which consists of two pages, bearing in the original format, ERN number 04358245, one page in Serbo-Croat and one corresponding translation page in English, is being received and marked as Defence Exhibit D763.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please show the witness Defence Exhibit D256?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a list of the 2nd Battalion. It's their salary list for the month of December. Witness, could you please look through the document and then turn to the last page, which bears the number 01320830.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that is page 18, also the last page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, have you found this part on the last page where it states, recapitulation?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at what it says underneath that? It says recapitulation, payment for soldiers of the 2nd Infantry Battalion for December 1992, and, look, it says battalion command, detachment I Jelav, detachment II Pobrdje, Drina detachment III, accompanying squad-mortar reconnaissance, and then it says, total 502 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, could you comment on this recapitulation or summary? Did you hear of the existence of these units before December 1992 or not?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. We did hear of all of these units through the communications. These are units from the local regions. Pobrdje, and Drinska, and companies were made in that area, and these are the same units that attacked Voljavica, Zaluzje, Biljaca, at the beginning, except that at the time they were called the TO units of a certain place, Jelav, Pobrdje, and so on, and then they had grown into proper companies and they had an accompanying mortar squad.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you a question in relation to that. When we are talking about mortars, did you hear anything through the radio about that?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: We constantly listened about the mortars, because they were always asking for mortar support over the radio. This helped us a lot to be able to seek shelter or move away whenever they asked for support.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please now look at page 013208220? That's page 8 in English. It's also page 8. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you look at the bottom of the page where it states squad from Kunjarac, and under 91 it says Andjelko Obrenovic, squad commander, Kunjarac squad. My question is: Did you hear of this person before? Did you know this person?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Andjelko Obrenovic was my maths teacher. He was born in Pobrdje. He worked in Bratunac. Later he started working in the elementary school in Voljavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know his voice?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew his voice very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was it his voice that you heard in the communications in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. course of October, November and December 1992?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard his voice many times in that period. I knew his voice very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at page 16 now? In the English version it's also page 16. It bears the number 01320828. And if you look at the top of the page, you can see that it states here: "Reconnaissance platoon" and underneath it says Bosko Neskovic. Did you hear anything about this in the communications that you were monitoring?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. We heard of Neskovic. They always said, can Crveni respond? He was called by the name Crveni, red. And he was very important to them because there were reservoirs for the local water supply there in Bratunac, and that's why Crveni had special units there at Kunjarac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Vidovic. I notice that in the transcript, the words reconnaissance platoon were used. In the document itself, we have reconnaissance squad, and then brackets, red and Perica. I'm raising this because you yourself have raised the matter in the past. You don't agree that the words platoon and squad ought to be used as meaning the same thing. And the second thing is -- in other words whether you accept that this was a platoon as translated to us during the interpretation. Second, what's the meaning of that Perica?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, the witness is better versed in these military questions and that's why I will ask him. Do you agree that in this document it says [B/C/S spoken], reconnaissance platoon?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the word is squad, according to how I understand it. "Vod" in B/C/S is platoon. In the original the words are [B/C/S spoken] vod.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm raising the matter. To us the only significance of all this is that in the past you have raised this distinction or pointed at this distinction between a squad and a platoon, and perhaps you can tell us exactly whether we are to accept platoon or whether we are to ignore the translation into squad as it appears on the document itself, in the English version of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we insist always that the word be translated the way it is in the Bosnian original. Sometimes the word "vod" is used and sometimes the word "odeljenje." In this case, in this document, the word used is "vod" so you cannot mix these two things simply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And according to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What does it mean according to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And to be perfectly honest, offhand I can't remember whether "vod" is platoon or squad. I think "vod" is platoon and "odeljenje" is squad, in which case it should be correctly translated as it has been on the transcript as platoon. And this exhibit would need to be corrected to that extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Jones. And Perica, what does Perica mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please help us whether Perica is a formation or something? Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: No. Perica was a man who was contacting with Crveni from Kunjarac. So he would frequently pick up when they talked with the Bratunac garrison. Sometimes they would ask for Perica and sometimes they would ask for Crveni.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, in our language, the word "Perica" signifies a name, Petar or Perica. It's a name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And what means "red" in this context? Is it indicating a colour or also a person or some unit or whatever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Crveni was a unit that was stationed in that area. The reconnaissance platoon had a code name, a symbolic name, Crveni, Reds, that's the name they gave themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Madam Vidovic. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were these the terms that you heard during these radio communications, just to clarify that?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. These were the terms that they used.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please show the witness another document now? It's number 0436999, and it's a document by the Bratunac garrison command of the 11th of October, 1992, sent to the Birac Brigade, to the command of the Birac Brigade. Could you please look at this document and focus on items 1, 2 and 3 of the document? I'm going to read item 1 to you. "Together with the forces from Kravica, we have laid strong ambushes in order to prevent fresh forces from Srebrenica from being brought into battle. In the course of today, the Voljavica-Pobrdje-Andrici line was moved, and we have joined up with the forces from Sase. In this way, we have considerably shortened the front line. We are also setting up the Bratunac-Glogova line at the Kaolin-Ladja, elevation 488, on positions Vresje [phoen], trig point 532, together with the Kravica forces. We have established communications according to the Kravica plan." I would like to ask the following based on that document: Did you have information about coordinated action between the forces from Kravica and these forces that you described a little bit earlier, in order to move the Voljavica-Pobrdje-Andrici line and its joining together with the Sase forces? But I would like to ask you just to give a little more time before you begin answering so that the interpreters could translate until the end. And you can reply now.

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: As soon as you heard the name of Jolje, Nikolic, Jovan being mentioned over the communications, we knew that these units were Kravica were helping these units in Pobrdje and that in joint action with them they were moving these lines towards Likari. By moving this line, the front towards Srebrenica became even tighter. Actually towards Likari, because Likari was the entry point to Srebrenica. And the departure of -- or actually, the forages of our civilians for food were becoming more and more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you the following: This movement of the Serb lines, Voljavica, Pobrdje, Andrici and joining together with the Sase forces, did this actually happen?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. This report fully reflects the situation in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could this document be given an exhibit number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The document that the Defence seeks to tender consists of one page in B/C/S which bears ERN number 04336999 and the corresponding translation into English which appears in two pages. The Trial Chamber points out, in case the Defence wishes to make any comments, that on the original B/C/S version, on the right-hand side of the document, there is an indication that this is a telegram or a telex. This does not -- is not reflected in the English translation. Also, in the original, just beneath the stamp, there are some words and a circle -- and a square which seem to be handwritten. I don't know what they mean but there is no corresponding entry in the English version. And also, in the original document, the bottom are the words [B/C/S spoken]. And this is also not repeated in the English version. In case any of this has any important -- importance for you, please feel free to make your comments. The document will be -- is being received and marked as Defence Exhibit D764. If the points that I raised are of any significance to you, please go ahead. If not, let's proceed with the next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, these are official translations. Thank you for pointing it out, and in the future I will pay attention to such details because it came from the official translation service, and it seems we need to check as to whether everything is contained in the translation. But this issue was not directly relevant to us. I guess we have given an exhibit number to this document already.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I wanted to ask you the following: Up until now, you have been describing the events until mid-October 1992 and the military situation in the field as you witnessed it or overheard it via radio communication. After mid-October of 1992, were there any other military activities in the -- in your area that you can remember?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I particularly remember that listening to their communication we learned of a strong offensive that was to be launched against Pirici and Poloznik, and there was a high concentration of our refugees there. We tried to tell that to the people there, as well as to Salihovic Midhat who was there with his group. We sent one lad who wanted to go there himself. His name was Samir Omerovic and his family was there somewhere, but unfortunately during those activities he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would kindly ask the usher to put a new document before the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, let's give this a number, Ms. Vidovic. This last document that has been made use of by the Defence consisting of, in the original language, one page with ERN number 04336995 and the corresponding translation into English is being tendered received and marked as Defence Exhibit D765.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you have the document before you?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at it. This is a document from the garrison command of Bratunac from the 13th of November of 1992. It is stated during the day, from 9.00 onwards an attack was conducted against Poloznik and Pirici. The enemy suffered great casualties. Until this moment we are positive about the 20 killed enemy soldiers as well as significant physical damage. Detailed report to follow tomorrow. Since the action is still ongoing. As of yesterday, in the village of Kravica and Kamenica, three enemy soldiers were killed in an ambush. I wanted to ask you the following regarding this. This document apparently was compiled by Captain Vaso Gujic [phoen]. Have you ever heard of that name before?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, several times. That was the person who usually contacted the troops in the field from the garrison command.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The attack on Pirici that you mentioned, does this document reflect the situation in the field mentioning the attack you mentioned when Samir Omerovic was killed?

utterances.speaker: AZIR MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. This report fully reflects the situation and the offensive as it was in mid-October. It lasted until the beginning of December. Pirici suffered strong attacks there as well as Podloznik and the various refugee camps and a lot of people were killed during those attacks. People were forced to withdraw further towards Prezovica [phoen] and together with the inhabitants of Podloznik and Pirici, and they remained there until early December.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe now is the time that you asked me to leave at your disposal. Thank you, Witness, for today. I believe we are finished for the day, continuing tomorrow. Did I understand properly, Your Honour, that this document has already been given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: D765. Mr. Malagic, we have to stop here today because we need to discuss a couple of other matters which do not concern you. So you will be now escorted out of the courtroom by Madam Usher. You will return again tomorrow to continue with your examination-in-chief and hopefully finish with it after which we will start with the cross-examination. In the meantime, please I wish to draw your attention to a very important matter. You are not to discuss with anyone between today and tomorrow, and that applies also for the following days, the subject matter of your testimony. It doesn't mean to say that you cannot ring up your family and say hello or receive calls from family or friends, et cetera, but the -- any discussion on the subject matter of your testimony or on this case in general is prohibited and you must not engage in it. Did I make myself clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You will return back tomorrow morning at 9.00. Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, there are two matters that need to be dealt with. Ms. Sellers, the matter that you wished to raise, is it going to be raised in public session or in private session?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Private session, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought you had mentioned that. So let's move into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. I thank you for your cooperation. These two matters will be handled in due course accordingly, and we can now adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.00, I think, in this same courtroom? No? In courtroom ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Courtroom III, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: be reconvened on Tuesday, the 27th day of September, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.
